We absolutely should. Not out of some misguided attempt to keep all species around forever, but as an indicator of the ecosystem's health.

Biodiversity is a measure of resilience and robustness of an ecosystem. The fewer species with overlapping niches there are, the harder an ecosystem will fall when environmental changes occur. If there are 'backup' species which can take over the niche of another, then nutrient cycles can continue to function while the ecosystem adjusts.

Species don't become endangered out of some innate inability to compete or because they're weak. It is external changes to their environment that cause their food supplies to dwindle. The specialist species are the first to go because they are the least adaptable, competition having driven them to specialize. Generalist species can adapt to more rapid changes (see foxes, skunks, racoons,, primates, rats/mice, and other urban "pests").

The problem with not caring about species die off is that it ignores a warning sign. The major extinction events in the past happened over several thousand years. We're in the middle of a low point in biodiversity and still species are disappearing faster than in any other mass extinction.

It's tempting to disregard endangered species as "weak" and let them die off, but it's not just animals; plants are also going extinct. Our agriculture is driving habitat loss and in place of the biodiverse ecosystem, we plant monocultures for harvesting ease. We're setting ourselves up for famine and ignoring the signs of a troubled ecosystem.
